background.definition: Erythema multiforme (EM) is usually a self-limited, mild skin disease characterized by symmetrically distributed lesions of the extremities and are associated with infections, most notably herpes simplex virus (HSV), or use of implicated medictions. The primary skin lesions are mainly papules with concentric color changes (target lesions), but can involve the mucous membranes in some cases. EM is no longer considered part of the immune-mediated spectrum that includes Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which are predominantly medication-induced.

list.listitem: Incidence: 0.01% to <1%
Erythema multiforme (EM) most often affects young adults, but can be seen in children and adolescents.
EM is slightly more common in females, but has no racial predilection.

Viral infections most notably due to Herpes simplex virus (HSV) types 1 and 2 among adults. Other associated viruses include hepatitis C virus (HCV), Epstein-Barr virus (HBV), influenza virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2).
Bacteria, most notably Mycoplasma pneumoniae among children. Other bacteria include Yersinia enterocolitica and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Fungal causes: Histoplasma, Candida spp.
Medications: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), antiepileptics, antibiotics (sulfonamides, penicillins), allopurinol
Other conditions: menstruation, complex apthosis, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), malignancies, polymorphous light eruption, high benzoic acid (food preservative) consumption

EM associated with HSV is caused by a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction involving the transport of viral DNA fragments on mononuclear cells and the expression of HSV genes within the fragments on keratinocytes. These lead to activation of HSV-specific CD4 helper T cells, which produce interferon gamma and lead to activation of the inflammatory cascade.
Drug-associated EM lesions involve activation of monocyte/macrophage produced tumor necrosis factor alpha instead of interferon.

list.listitem: Consider a diagnosis of erythema multiforme (EM) among patients presenting with mostly cutaneous (sometimes mucosal) fixed targetoid lesions along the acral skin, especially in the setting of herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection among young adults or, less commonly, the use of EM-associated medications.
EM is no longer considered part of the immune-mediated spectrum that includes Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which are predominantly medication-induced.

Differentiate EM minor (cutaneous manifestations only) from EM major (mucosal involvement with or without prodromal symptoms) to assist with therapeutic choices. Additionally, identify acute EM, recurrent EM (≥4-6 episodes per year), and persistent EM given the implications to management and prognosis.

EM presents mostly with typical target lesions (3 concentric rings, with a central crust or bulla) and, occasionally, atypical target lesions (2 concentric rings). In EM, typical target lesions that appear papular (raised) are the predominant primary lesions. In contrast, SJS presents with flat (macular) dusky atypical target lesions.
Initial rash is symmetrically distributed along acral skin (palms, soles) and extensor surface of extremities, and may spread centripetally.

Mucosal EM commonly affects the oral cavity, but can also involve the genital, ocular, and respiratory mucosa. Systemic or prodromal symptoms of fever, fatigue, malaise, and myalgia commonly accompany mucosal EM. While there may be similarities between the mucosal findings of EM major and SJS/TEN, the current thinking is that EM is a distinct diagnostic entity that carries no risk of progression to SJS/TEN.
EM is a clinical diagnosis; diagnostic testing such as biopsy should be limited to searching for other possible causes of the skin lesions in complicated cases.
Complicated cases include patients with extensive lesions or cases that persist for more than 6 weeks.

In 32 patients (13 with EM and 10 with SJS/TEN) and 15 matched controls, serum IL-17 levels were significantly raised in the EM group (35 ± 24 pg/ml, p <0.02) and SJS/TEN group (68 ± 35 pg/ml, p = 0.0001). IL-17 was also significantly raised in SJS/TEN group compared to EM group (p = 0.004). Serum IL-17 correlated with both percentage surface area detached skin and SCORTEN.
Suspect EM in patients with fixed target lesions symmetrically affecting the acral skin and extremities with a recent relevant infection or drug exposure.
Diagnostic testing is not required, except to look for alternative causes or diagnoses.
Treatment is supportive for most cases, but topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines can be used to treat mild acute EM.
Mild acute EM is usually self-limited and may not require treatment. C
Treat any underlying infection (eg, herpes labialis); stop any inciting medication (eg, antibiotics, NSAIDs, antiepileptics, allopurinol). C
Symptomatic patients with mild to moderate acute EM may be treated with topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and topical antiseptics. C

Treat mild to moderate oral mucosal involvement with high-potency topical corticosteroid gel, oral anesthetic solutions, and oral antiseptic washes. Patients with severe oral involvement preventing adequate hydration or nutrition may need to be hospitalized for intravenous hydration, electrolyte repletion, and systemic corticosteroid therapy. C
The first-line treatment for both HSV-associated and idiopathic recurrent EM involves suppressive oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for at least six months. B

For antiviral-refractory cases of recurrent or persistent EM, consider other systemic therapies including antibiotics (azithromycin, dapsone), antihelmintics (levamisole), antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine), corticosteroids (prednisone), and immunomodulators (thalidomide, adalimumab, rituximab, apremilast, azathioprine, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, immunoglobulin). C
A systematic review in 2019 identified only one RCT (n=20) and six case series evaluating the effectiveness of pharmacologic therapies for EM.
Mild acute EM is usually self-limited and may not require treatment.

If an etiology is identified, it should be addressed. For instance, any underlying infection should be treated (eg, prescribe antivirals for adults with herpes labialis or antibiotics for children with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection). Similarly, if a medication is suspected as the cause, it should be discontinued. While this is common practice, newer literature has not found evidence that treating HSV-induced acute EM with oral antivirals shortens the duration of symptoms or hastens the resolution of lesions.
Symptomatic patients with mild to moderate cutaneous EM may be treated with topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and topical antiseptics.

EM-like lesions have been reported in patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, but there is uncertainty whether the infection or the medications used to treat it are the cause. Cessation of SARS-CoV-2 antiviral therapy and a tapered course of systemic corticosteroids are recommended for mild to moderate EM.
Treat mild to moderate mucosal involvement with high-potency topical corticosteroid gel, oral anesthetic solutions, and oral antiseptic washes.
Patients with severe mucosal involvement preventing adequate hydration or nutrition may need to be hospitalized for intravenous hydration, electrolyte repletion, and systemic corticosteroid therapy.
Immediate ophthalmology consultation is warranted for patients with ocular involvement. Treatment usually consists of antibiotic and corticosteroid eyedrops, as well as eye lubricants.
Recurrent EM is a challenging condition to treat as it is usually refractory to treatment.

Based on the only RCT (n=20) evaluating oral antiviral therapy for recurrent EM, the first-line treatment for both HSV-associated and idiopathic recurrent EM involves oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for at least six months. The treatment group had a recurrence rate of 36%, whereas the control group had a 100% recurrence rate (NNT = 1.6). In the acyclovir-treated group, 9 of 11 patients had EM attributable to HSV. Of the two patients in the acyclovir-treated group deemed from an idiopathic cause, one had complete disease suppression while on oral antiviral therapy. It is thought that many patients with idiopathic recurrent EM may have subclinical HSV infection, hence the response to suppressive antiviral therapy.

For patients with recurrent EM unresponsive to suppressive oral acyclovir therapy, doubling the dose or switching to another antiviral is recommended. Alternative oral antivirals include valacyclovir 500mg twice daily and famciclovir 250mg twice daily.

Based on retrospective studies of recurrent EM, and due to high recurrence rates after cessation of 6 months of suppressive antiviral therapy, some experts recommend suppressive therapy for 1 to 2 years. And if recurrence occurs after this, trying another 6 to 12 months of suppressive therapy may be warranted before considering discontinuation.

For antiviral-refractory cases, consider other systemic therapies, based on weak data from case series and expert opinion. Options include antibiotics (azithromycin, dapsone), antihelmintics (levamisole), antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine), corticosteroids (prednisone), and immunomodulatory drugs (thalidomide, adalimumab, rituximab, apremilast, azathioprine, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, immunoglobulin).

Persistent EM is a rare but debilitating disease, defined as continuous EM or ≤15 days disease-free period between flares. It has been associated with HSV, HCV, CMV, influenza virus, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancies.
Treatment is similar to recurrent EM, with oral antiviral suppressive therapy as first-line therapy, and various systemic therapies for antiviral-refractory cases (see above).
Treatment is generally symptomatic, with analgesics and cold compresses as needed for mild cases.
Although not common, be vigilant for secondary bacterial infection of cuteneous lesions.
Consider dermatology referral for recurrent or persistent EM, and patients with moderate to severe disease especially with mucosal involvement.
Immediately refer patients with ocular EM to ophthalmology.
Consider hospitalization for cases in patients at the extremes of age, and for patients with oral EM unable to keep hydration or nutrition.
Acute EM is a self-limited disease that generally lasts 1 to 4 weeks for mild cases, but may last up to 6 weeks for severe cases especially those with mucosal involvement. C
Newer literature suggests that treatment of HSV-induced acute EM with oral antivirals does not shorten the duration of symptoms nor hasten the resolution of lesions. C

Without treatment, patients with recurrent EM, on average, experience 6 outbreaks per year, with the disease lasting 6 to 10 years. Although sometimes difficult to achieve, the goal of suppressive or systemic therapy is to induce remission. C
Persistent EM is a rare, refractory, debilitating disease characterized by chronic, continuous disease or ≤15 days of disease-free period between flares. C
